## AI

### <span class="imp imp-high" title="Importance 7.5/10" aria-label="Importance 7.5 of 10">7.5</span> African Laboratory Warns on AI-Generated Bioweapons Risk
MinoHealth AI Labs in Ghana, led by founder Darlington Akogo, jailbroke their own drug discovery language model in 2024 to test its safety boundaries by asking it to design toxins. The model generated designs for 1,020 proteins and 5,000 small molecules, with software predicting all as likely toxic; some resembled ricin. The research was uploaded to arXiv in May 2025. Akogo raised concerns about dual-use risks, specifically whether someone could take such designs to DNA synthesis companies undetected. The findings have been discussed within Interpol and at high-level forums including World Bank/IMF meetings. Bill Gates, in conversation with Akogo in 2023, has since issued public warnings; in September 2026 he stated on The Ezra Klein Show that AI has crossed the threshold where it can empower bioterrorists to kill hundreds of millions. Kenya's Ministry of Information official Brenda Obuya indicated the need to regulate DNA synthesis providers is now being discussed at the highest levels of Kenyan government. Experts note that since the study, LLM capabilities have increased and barriers to entry lowered, raising risks of lay users generating similar outputs via chatbots.

## Security

### <span class="imp imp-high" title="Importance 7/10" aria-label="Importance 7 of 10">7</span> Enterprise LLM access stolen and resold at low cost in emerging black market
Criminal actors are exploiting 'LLM Mixers' — underground gateways — to steal and resell enterprise AI access credentials at drastically reduced prices. According to Google's Q4 AI Threat Tracker from the Google Threat Intelligence Group, stolen AI token batches are being sold for as little as $0.10, while the targeted organizations continue to foot usage bills that can exceed $100,000. The theft method, called LLMjacking, involves stealing AI-related credentials including usernames, passwords, and API keys used to access large language models. Once compromised, unauthorized users can run high-resource computing tasks, deploy malicious AI systems, or extract corporate data from the AI's memory. The report notes that organizations vary widely in monthly AI spending — the top 1% of firms spend over $10,000 per employee per month, while the median firm spends around $16 per employee per month. Many smaller organizations may lack spending caps on AI access, making them vulnerable. Recommended defenses include implementing spending caps, setting up suspicious behavior alerts, and increased vigilance.

Sources: [ZDNET](https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMiiAFBVV95cUxPcFBRNHY3cnBuZ3JsUFJjUkFrd0l6X3c5WFc1eXYxNE9KdjY3MWd2dHZGTTVXcFJ2X1hZWmxmQi1CQ3paaXVCUE9MMDJ1YTR2eHdrMUdIVUVLUDdSSmRoS0dPdFcySGp0VGl0YnY1WHVRdEduRUlZcEZ3djBHaHpjeTVhT1UzV0hz?oc=5) <span class="src-badge src-research">AI Web Searched</span>
